summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a static web app that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates side by side in seconds. Pick up to four site-and-date scenarios, press Play, and watch the Sun and Earth move across each site's real terrain horizon. The horizons are computed from NASA LOLA elevation models (720 rays, Moon curvature included), and Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, hourly from December 2026 to December 2028. Every card shows Sun visible %, the longest dark stretch, Earth in view % and countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset. A ±60-day slip slider, a window finder and a 3D surface view with a movable lander answer "same site, new date" and "same date, nearby site" without opening Horizons or a GIS. The library holds 21 sourced sites: Apollo, CLPS, China, India, Japan, the Soviet Union and Russia, plus NASA's Artemis candidate regions. Simple mode explains the polar extremes in plain language. One example: at the IM-2 south-pole site, slipping a 14-day mission by 14 days moves Sun visible from 6.8 % to 94.0 %. All 43 validation checks pass.
details:
What it does

Lunar Landing Site Navigator shows where the Sun and Earth are relative to the real local horizon at a lunar site, and counts how much of a chosen window each is above it. Up to four site-and-date scenario cards sit side by side and play in step on one timeline, so "same site, new date" and "same date, nearby site" become one-click comparisons. The app opens on a south-pole scenario, and the Apollo 11 vs South Pole preset puts the equator and the pole next to each other. Try it live: https://michalszaumkesel.github.io/Lunar-Landing-Site-Navigator/

How it works

  • Data pipeline (Python, offline). The pipeline reads NASA LOLA elevation models from the PDS Geosciences Node. Polar demo sites use LDEM_80S_20M (20 m/px); other polar sites use LDEM_80S_40M or LDEM_75S_60M; Apollo 11 uses LDEM_1024 (about 30 m); the other library sites use LDEM_256 (about 118 m). Polar DEMs are indexed in Moon-sphere polar stereographic coordinates.
  • Horizon masks. Each site gets 720 rays (0.5° apart) over 100 km (150 km at the pole). The angle to each terrain point is atan2(h − (h0 + observer) − d²/2R, d), which includes the curvature drop, and the horizon is the maximum along each ray. Observer heights are 2 m and 10 m.
  • Ephemeris. JPL Horizons gives the Sun and Earth from an observer on the Moon at the site: apparent azimuth and elevation, no refraction, hourly from 2026-12-01 to 2028-12-31 (18,288 samples). Libration and Moon orientation come from Horizons and are not re-implemented.
  • Metrics. One contract defines Sun visible (disc centre above the horizon), Earth in view, longest dark stretch, visible solar-disc fraction and sunset/Earthset countdowns, implemented in both Python and TypeScript.
  • Validation: 43 of 43 checks pass. Ephemeris files match a fresh Horizons query within 0.0012° at 13 sites. Crater bowls in our DEM lie 0.3–1.7 km from the IAU/USGS centres of Shackleton, Shoemaker and de Gerlache. Sun and Earth shares agree with NASA PGDA polar illumination maps within 1.7 percentage points at two south-pole sites (local grids: r = 0.98). TypeScript metrics match Python to 5.7e-14 on 180 real values. Horizon uncertainty is estimated per site.

Features

  • Scenario board (up to 4 cards), compare table, 2 m / 10 m observer switch.
  • Play at 1–168 h per second, ±60-day slip slider, slip tolerance strip.
  • Polar sky plot and panorama on the real horizon, solar-disc loupe, elevation chart.
  • 3D terrain with live shadows, a movable lander, a Sunlight map and "Find spot with most Sun visible".
  • Mission rules, window finder (site × date matrix), Moon map, 21-site library with sources.
  • Share links, CSV export, print dossier, "Copy Horizons query".
  • Simple and Advanced modes, guided tour, keyboard access, reduced motion.

Benefits & impact

  • Planners re-check a slipped date or a nearby site in seconds. At the IM-2 site, a 14-day slip moves a 14-day mission from 6.8 % to 94.0 % Sun visible.
  • Educators get Simple mode with plain-language summaries. At the IM-2 site the Sun never rises above 6.8°.
  • The public can play time forward and watch a ridge cut the solar disc.

Creativity

The real jagged horizon is the backdrop for every view: a loupe shows the solar disc being clipped, you can stand on the terrain and lock the camera on the Sun, and the slip strip shows how a result changes with the date, not just one value.

Tools & languages

TypeScript, React, Vite, D3 and three.js for the web app. Python with numpy, rasterio and pyproj for the pipeline. Vitest and pytest for tests, and GitHub Actions for builds.

Limitations & honesty

  • "Sun visible" is not power (panel angle, dust, temperature, battery are not modelled). "Earth in view" is not a radio link (antennas, schedules, ground stations are not modelled). Both are geometric line-of-sight tests on the disc centre.
  • Two years of data, not the 18.6-year cycle. DEM resolution 20–118 m, so boulders and small rims are missing.
  • The disc cut assumes a straight horizon across the disc.
  • Custom coordinates without the optional service are approximated and labelled "Approximate".
  • The ephemeris check confirms our files against Horizons; it is not an independent model. No published horizon profiles were found to check ours against.

LOLA LDEM_80S_20M (south polar DEM, 20 m/px): demo polar sites, local sunlight grids, crater orientation check
LOLA LDEM_80S_40M (south polar DEM, 40 m/px): polar sites, south-pole map background
LOLA LDEM_75S_60M (south polar DEM, 60 m/px): polar sites
LOLA LDEM_1024 (global DEM, about 30 m/px): Apollo 11 horizon and terrain
LOLA LDEM_256 (global DEM, about 118 m/px): other library sites
JPL Horizons API: Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation per site, Earth orientation
NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit: global map background (credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio)
NASA Blue Marble: Earth disc texture in the 3D view (credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; Reto Stockli, Robert Simmon)
NASA NSSDCA lunar landing sites (Apollo 12–17 coordinates)
NASA NSSDCA lunar artifact impacts (Hakuto-R M1, Chang'e 3, Luna 9, Luna 25 coordinates)
LRO Camera (LROC) site images: landing coordinates (IM-2, IM-1, Blue Ghost, Chang'e 4/5/6, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Apollo 11)
LROC NAC mosaics: Artemis candidate region points (Mons Mouton Plateau, Malapert, Haworth)
NASA: update on Artemis III Moon landing regions (2024 list of 9)
NASA NTRS: LPSC 2026 abstract confirming the 9 candidate regions
NASA: IM-2 landing closest to the south pole
NASA History SP-4214, Apollo landing times
NASA NTRS: Mazarico et al. polar illumination (reference values)
projectRefs: USGS/IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: crater centres for the orientation check
Gläser et al. 2014 (DLR): south-pole illumination reference
Gläser et al. 2018 (DLR): south-pole illumination reference
